newsitem.title: USA: Violence erupts after Florida officer cleared.
newsitem.headline: Violence erupts after Florida officer cleared.

text.p: An officer was shot and police used tear gas to disperse small bands of angry youths Wednesday, hours after a grand jury ruled that a white police officer was justified in killing a black motorist whose death sparked a night of rioting.

The officer was shot in the leg after police responded to a report of gunfire in south St. Petersburg, a predominantly black section of the city rocked by rioting on Oct. 24, St. Petersburg police spokesman Bill Doniel said.
The officers were subjected to rock and bottle throwing and then more shots were fired, one of them striking Officer Keith Glasgow, 39, in the left leg, Doniel said.
"He's doing fine," Maj. Cedric Gordon told reporters after a visit to the hospital where Glasgow, an 18-year veteran of the force, was being treated.

Police stepped up patrols in the neighbourhood after the grand jury ruled that Officer James Knight was justified in the fatal shooting of motorist Tyron Lewis, 18, following a routine traffic stop three weeks ago.

The shooting was followed by hours of rioting in south St. Petersburg. At least 11 people were hurt, mostly police officers, and nearly 30 fires were set in shops, businesses and homes before police regained control of the streets early the next morning.
"We have determined the death of Tyron Lewis was the result of a justifiable homicide under Florida law," Pinellas County State Attorney Bernie McCabe said after the 16-member grand jury acted.
Following the grand jury ruling, the police department suspended Knight for 60 days without pay for violating its firearms policy. Knight's attorney, Joseph Ciarciaglino, said he would appeal.

But the grand jury ruled the death of Lewis was justifiable homicide because Knight was in danger of being run over by the car Lewis was driving after he and his partner, Sandra Minor, pulled Lewis over for speeding.

Knight, 34, appeared before the grand jury on Tuesday to provide his account. He has been on administrative leave since the shooting. Minor, one of the first witnesses to testify in the case, returned on Tuesday to testify a second time.

Black youths in the city charged they were constantly victimised by police. Community leaders said poverty, lack of jobs and bleak prospects for blacks in St. Petersburg created resentment that fuelled the unrest. The incident also prompted federal investigations.
Officials had stepped up the police presence in the riot area Wednesday night, where community reaction to the ruling was mixed.
Truman Smith, who raised Lewis, said of the ruling: "To kill my son and then to clear the officer is unthinkable."
Erica Serrmons, a black worker at a barbecue shop across the road from the scene of the shooting, said the ruling could have been unfair because the grand jury had only one black.

"Most people here, young people especially, feel the decision was not good enough," Serrmons said. "But I suppose that he was investigated and if the process was fair then it should be accepted by the public."
